# Contributing to PAIR

Everything arrives as a pull request. You do not need write access to this repository, and
nobody is expected to have it.

## Adding an initiative

### With the tool

```sh
pair add https://example.org/the-thing
```

This reads the page or repository, drafts `initiatives/<id>.yaml`, and tells you what it had
to guess.

**Read the draft before you submit it.** It is generated by a language model and it will get
things wrong, particularly `capabilities`, where it tends to restate marketing copy instead of
describing what a person can actually do. An entry that overstates a tool's abilities will send
someone down a dead end and stop them building the thing themselves. That is a worse outcome
than a missing entry.

Then validate:

```sh
pair check
```

### By hand

Copy the example from [SPEC.md §4.1](SPEC.md#41-example) into
`initiatives/<your-id>.yaml` and fill it in. The tool is a convenience, not a requirement.

### Then

1. Fork, branch, commit your single new file.
2. Open a pull request.
3. CI runs the validator. Fix anything it flags.
4. A maintainer reviews and merges.

One initiative per pull request, please. It keeps review fast and makes the history readable.

## Writing good capabilities

This is the only part of an entry that is genuinely hard, and it determines whether anyone
ever finds your initiative.

Write what a person can **do**, in the words they would use. Not what the system is, not how
it was built.

Good:

```yaml
capabilities:
  - Check how much my city spent on road repairs last year
  - Get notified when a new budget document is published for my area
  - Download the raw spending data as a spreadsheet
```

Bad:

```yaml
capabilities:
  - Fiscal transparency dashboard          # that is a category, not an action
  - Nightly ETL from the treasury portal   # implementation, invisible to users
  - The most complete budget tool around   # promotional, unverifiable
```

A useful test: would someone type something close to this line into a search box while trying
to solve their actual problem? If not, rewrite it.

Three to five capabilities is usually right. One is thin. Ten is a sign the initiative does
several things that might be separate entries.

## Honesty rules

These are the ones maintainers will actually push back on.

- **`status` must be true today.** If it is not usable by the public right now, it is not
  `live`. Half-finished is `building`. An unstarted plan is `idea`. There is no shame in any
  of these, and an honest `idea` entry is how you find collaborators.
- **Do not claim capabilities you have not shipped.** Planned features belong in a roadmap,
  not in a registry someone is using to decide whether to build.
- **Scope must match reality.** A tool serving one city is not `national`.
- **Declare your interest.** If you are submitting your own initiative, say so in the pull
  request. That is welcome and normal, it just should not be hidden.

## Updating an entry

Anyone can update any entry, not just the person who added it. If you confirmed an entry is
still accurate, bump `last_verified` to today and open a pull request. That is a small,
genuinely valuable contribution, and the registry depends on people doing it.

If you are correcting someone else's entry with information they would dispute, say where your
information came from in the pull request.

## When an initiative dies

Do not delete the file. Set `status: dormant` and bump `last_verified`.

The record that something was attempted, by whom, and that it stopped, is useful. It tells the
next person the idea is viable, who to ask about it, and what went wrong. Deleting it throws
that away and guarantees the same ground gets covered again.

If the initiative was replaced by or merged into another, also set `superseded_by` to that
entry's `id`.

## What maintainers check

The validator handles structure, so review is only about things a machine cannot judge:

- Is this a real, identifiable initiative?
- Do the capabilities describe what a person can do, in plain language?
- Is `status` honest?
- Is this a duplicate of an existing entry, or genuinely distinct?

Reviews should be quick. If a pull request sits, nudge it.

## Licensing your contribution

By submitting an entry or an edit, you agree to place it under
[CC0 1.0](LICENSE), the same terms as the rest of the registry. In plain terms, you are putting
the text you wrote into the public domain so anyone can reuse it without asking.

This applies to the entry text you write, not to the initiative it describes. Nothing here
affects the licence of your own project.

## Reporting a problem without opening a pull request

Open an issue. A broken link, a stale entry, or an initiative you know about but do not have
time to write up are all worth reporting. Someone else can do the writing.
